name: Enterprise AI Platforms & Agent Orchestration
intro:
Enterprise AI platforms and agent orchestration covers software whose product is the agent layer itself: platforms that let a company deploy, connect, and govern AI agents across its own systems, as opposed to a single-purpose AI feature inside one application. The boundary is horizontality. This category excludes point tools that do one task well, and it excludes the embedded AI inside ERP or HR systems covered elsewhere on the site. What belongs here spans two related jobs, customer-facing conversational agents and internal enterprise knowledge and service automation: Aisera, Cognigy, Decagon, Glean, Kore.ai, Moveworks, Sierra, and Vellum.

A buyer here is choosing an orchestration layer, not a single model. Sierra and Decagon both build customer-facing support agents, model-agnostic and omnichannel by design. Glean and Moveworks build internal knowledge and IT service agents that sit on top of a company's existing tools with permission-aware retrieval. Kore.ai and Aisera position themselves as full multi-agent orchestration platforms with governance dashboards, audit logs, and role-based access built in, while Cognigy focuses on GDPR-compliant, EU-hosted conversational deployment.

Capital flowed into this category faster than almost any other over the past year, which is itself the story. Sierra raised 950 million dollars at a 15 billion dollar valuation in May 2026. Decagon tripled its valuation to 4.5 billion dollars in a 250 million dollar round in early 2026, after raising at 1.5 billion just seven months earlier. Glean raised 150 million dollars at a 7.2 billion dollar valuation in mid-2025. That pace of funding reflects enterprise buyers actively replacing pilot chatbots with governed, production agent platforms.

Sierra and Decagon are the clearest reference points for customer-facing agents given their funding and scale, while Glean is the reference point for internal enterprise search and knowledge agents.

reading.body:
Enterprise AI platforms are consolidating around governance, multi-agent orchestration, and permission-aware data access as core requirements rather than optional features.

The category divides into two practical streams. One builds autonomous agents for specific enterprise functions: service desks, customer support, employee help, and knowledge retrieval. The other provides orchestration infrastructure to manage multiple agents, enforce access controls, and maintain audit trails. Kore.ai explicitly names multi-agent orchestration and governance dashboards. Glean and Moveworks emphasize permission-aware retrieval and access controls. This reflects a market maturity constraint: enterprises will not deploy AI agents at scale without visibility into what data each agent accesses and what actions it takes.

Governance features appear across nearly every tool because they solve a real problem that scales with agent deployment. RBAC, audit logs, and guardrails are not marketing additions; they are prerequisites for regulatory compliance and operational safety in large organizations. Cognigy's GDPR compliance and EU hosting options indicate that jurisdiction and data residency requirements shape the market geography.

The data does not reveal compute consumption, infrastructure costs, or how much processing each platform demands. It does not show whether orchestration overhead meaningfully increases total computational load compared to single-agent deployments. For that, you would need infrastructure telemetry, not feature lists.
